Chapter 1

From particles to bulk behavior

I begin with a glass of water rather than an exotic material. Its molecules have positions, momenta, and interactions. The glass also has a temperature, a pressure, a viscosity, and a surface that rounds small drops. None of those macroscopic descriptions can be assigned to one isolated water molecule in the same operational sense. The task is to show how the descriptions become reliable, and which microscopic information they retain.

The first three entries develop equilibrium bookkeeping: temperature governs energy exchange, pressure records momentum transfer, and entropy counts the microscopic possibilities compatible with a macroscopic preparation. Diffusion, sound, and viscosity then ask how disturbances move or decay. Elasticity and surface tension introduce free-energy costs associated with deformation and interfaces. Screening shows why a force measured inside a material already includes the rearrangement of its surroundings.

Hydrodynamics gathers these ideas into a general strategy. I retain slow fields, use conservation to constrain their evolution, and put unresolved microscopic processes into measurable material coefficients. This is a particularly concrete form of emergence: a change in the variables and laws useful at a chosen scale. It does not require a sharp phase transition, and it does not mean that every microscopic detail becomes irrelevant. Each entry identifies the assumptions that make the reduction work.

01Temperature: Why two different thermometers agree

Established phenomenon · coarse graining · conservation

I put a gas thermometer and a small metal thermometer into the same insulated bath. Their atoms, energy spectra, and readouts differ, yet after equilibration they identify one temperature. The puzzle is why a single number can describe energy exchange between such unlike systems. Temperature is not the energy of an average atom: molecules may store energy in rotation, vibration, interactions, and other degrees of freedom.

I begin with two weakly coupled bodies that exchange energy while their combined energy stays fixed. Let ΩA(EA)\Omega_A(E_A)ΩA​(EA​) count the microscopic states compatible with the macroscopic constraints on body AAA, and define its entropy by SA=kBln⁡ΩAS_A=k_B\ln\Omega_ASA​=kB​lnΩA​, where kBk_BkB​ is Boltzmann's constant. The number of combined states is approximately the product ΩA(EA)ΩB(E−EA)\Omega_A(E_A)\Omega_B(E-E_A)ΩA​(EA​)ΩB​(E−EA​). At its maximum,

∂SA∂EA=∂SB∂EB,1T=(∂S∂E)V,N.\frac{\partial S_A}{\partial E_A}=\frac{\partial S_B}{\partial E_B},\qquad \frac1T=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial E}\right)_{V,N}.∂EA​∂SA​​=∂EB​∂SB​​,T1​=(∂E∂S​)V,N​.

Here VVV is volume and NNN particle number; both are held fixed. The quantity equalized by energy exchange is the entropy slope, which defines reciprocal absolute temperature. Many microscopic energy distributions therefore share the same criterion for equilibrium. A thermometer works because its own measurable property can be calibrated against this common parameter.

For a small system coupled to a much larger bath, expanding the bath entropy to first order in the exchanged energy gives a state probability proportional to e−Ei/(kBT)e^{-E_i/(k_BT)}e−Ei​/(kB​T), where EiE_iEi​ is the small system's state energy. This is the Boltzmann distribution. It explains why the same temperature controls a gas's velocity distribution and a spin's level populations without assigning them the same total energy. Classical quadratic degrees of freedom each contribute mean energy kBT/2k_BT/2kB​T/2; quantum level spacing limits that particular rule.

The construction requires an equilibrium description and adequate time for energy exchange. A driven sample may have different distributions for electrons and atomic vibrations, or no useful single temperature. Even at equilibrium, strong coupling complicates the separation into body and thermometer. What emerges is a transferable parameter for a specified class of exchanges, supported by the overwhelming concentration of accessible states around equilibrium.

Something I can try asking. Which observable would reveal that a sample fitted by one thermometer temperature is not actually in thermal equilibrium?

Sources and what they establish
  • Tong, Statistical Physics, §1.2.2 and §1.3. Authoritative lecture derivation of temperature from entropy maximization and the canonical distribution; equilibrium assumptions apply.

02Pressure: From molecular impacts to a smooth force

Established phenomenon · coarse graining · conservation

A piston feels a nearly steady push even though a dilute gas strikes it in separate, irregular impacts. I want to know how those impacts become pressure, a force per unit area that remains useful without tracking individual molecules. The key observable is momentum crossing a surface, averaged over an area and a time large compared with molecular scales.

Take NNN noninteracting particles of mass mmm in a rectangular box of volume VVV. A particle with velocity component vxv_xvx​ reverses its normal momentum on a reflecting wall, transferring 2m∣vx∣2m|v_x|2m∣vx​∣. Its return time to that wall is 2Lx/∣vx∣2L_x/|v_x|2Lx​/∣vx​∣, with LxL_xLx​ the box length. Dividing the average force by wall area and summing particles gives

p=NmV⟨vx2⟩=Nm3V⟨v2⟩.p=\frac{Nm}{V}\langle v_x^2\rangle=\frac{Nm}{3V}\langle v^2\rangle.p=VNm​⟨vx2​⟩=3VNm​⟨v2⟩.

The second equality uses an isotropic velocity distribution: no direction is preferred. With the equilibrium classical result m⟨v2⟩=3kBTm\langle v^2\rangle=3k_BTm⟨v2⟩=3kB​T, this becomes pV=NkBTpV=Nk_BTpV=NkB​T. Here kBk_BkB​ is Boltzmann's constant. Temperature TTT and number density N/VN/VN/V together determine the mean push. The wall records microscopic momentum transfer; it does not create the pressure.

I can imagine an internal plane through the gas and repeat the momentum accounting. Particles crossing it transport momentum between neighboring regions. In equilibrium this transport has equal normal components in every direction. Away from equilibrium, different components need not agree, and a stress tensor is needed: it records which component of force acts across a surface of each orientation. Interactions also carry momentum across the plane, so the ideal-gas formula cannot be applied unchanged to a dense liquid. The thermodynamic counterpart, p=−(∂F/∂V)T,Np=-(\partial F/\partial V)_{T,N}p=−(∂F/∂V)T,N​, follows from the reversible work of changing volume; FFF is Helmholtz free energy.

The smooth description is an averaging limit. A sufficiently small sensor resolves fluctuations, and a rapidly driven gas may retain directional velocity differences. Macroscopic pressure is therefore neither an extra microscopic force nor merely a name for collisions. It is a compact description of momentum transfer whose scalar form depends on local isotropy. Its success lets me predict piston motion without predicting the next collision.

Something I can try asking. When would a single pressure reading fail to describe the force exerted on differently oriented surfaces?

Sources and what they establish
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, I §39–2. Textbook derivation of dilute-gas pressure as momentum transfer and the ideal-gas equation of state.

03Entropy: Why mixing has a direction

Established phenomenon · coarse graining · constraints

I remove a partition that confines a gas to half a box. The particles obey reversible microscopic laws, yet the gas spreads and does not normally gather back into its original half. The interesting question is not whether a reversed trajectory exists. It does. The question is why almost every microscopic preparation compatible with the initial macroscopic conditions produces the same direction of change.

A macrostate specifies a limited set of observables, such as particle counts in spatial cells. A microstate specifies the detailed particle positions and momenta. Boltzmann entropy assigns SB=kBln⁡ΩS_B=k_B\ln\OmegaSB​=kB​lnΩ to a macrostate containing Ω\OmegaΩ compatible microstates; kBk_BkB​ is Boltzmann's constant. For an ideal gas, opening the other half roughly doubles each particle's accessible position volume. Thus the equilibrium entropy difference is

ΔSB=NkBln⁡2.\Delta S_B=Nk_B\ln 2.ΔSB​=NkB​ln2.

Here NNN is the particle number, and energy and total volume after expansion are fixed. At equilibrium, independent uniformly distributed positions put all particles in the original half with probability 2−N2^{-N}2−N. That probability measures the rarity of the old configuration; it is not a proof of a particular equilibration time.

I now have to keep two entropies distinct. For a classical probability density ρ\rhoρ on phase space, the fine-grained Gibbs entropy −kB∫ρln⁡ρ dΓ-k_B\int\rho\ln\rho\,d\Gamma−kB​∫ρlnρdΓ stays constant under Hamiltonian evolution, with a fixed reference measure understood. The evolving distribution stretches into detailed correlations. A coarse observation ignores those correlations and assigns growing weight to larger macrostates. For an isolated quantum system, the analogous full-state von Neumann entropy is likewise unchanged by unitary evolution, although the entropy of a subsystem may increase as it becomes entangled with its surroundings.

Entropy increase consequently needs both the chosen macroscopic description and an initially special preparation. Reversibility alone cannot select a time direction, and coarse-graining alone cannot guarantee that every trajectory relaxes. Integrable systems, which possess unusually many conserved quantities, and poorly mixing dynamics need additional care. In ordinary equilibrating matter, microscopic correlations become inaccessible to the selected measurements, while large-volume macrostates dominate what those measurements report. The emergent regularity is probabilistic irreversibility at the observational scale, with precisely stated exceptions rather than a violation of mechanics.

Something I can try asking. Which microscopic correlations would have to be controlled to reverse a gas expansion while keeping its macroscopic energy unchanged?

Sources and what they establish
  • Tong, Statistical Physics, §1.2.1 and §1.3.3. Lecture definitions of Boltzmann and Gibbs entropy; the distinction between microscopic reversibility and coarse observations is developed explicitly here.

04Diffusion: How aimless steps make a predictable profile

Established phenomenon · coarse graining · conservation

A spot of dye spreads through still water even though no molecule consults the concentration gradient. I start with a simpler puzzle: a walker steps left or right by distance aaa every time interval τ\tauτ, with independent equal probabilities. Each trajectory looks erratic. Nevertheless, after nnn steps its mean displacement is zero and its mean squared displacement is na2na^2na2. Predictability appears in the distribution, not in an individual path.

Let P(x,t)P(x,t)P(x,t) be the probability density of position. The discrete update averages the two neighboring values. Expanding over distances much larger than aaa and times much longer than τ\tauτ gives

∂tP=D∂x2P,D=a22τ,⟨x2⟩=2Dt.\partial_tP=D\partial_x^2P,\qquad D=\frac{a^2}{2\tau},\qquad \langle x^2\rangle=2Dt.∂t​P=D∂x2​P,D=2τa2​,⟨x2⟩=2Dt.

The diffusion coefficient DDD has units of area per time. A sharply localized initial distribution becomes a Gaussian of width proportional to t\sqrt{t}t​. Doubling a diffusion distance therefore requires four times as long. The same equation can describe the concentration ccc of many independent particles because their probabilities add.

For material transport, conservation supplies ∂tc+∇ ⁣⋅j=0\partial_tc+\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf j=0∂t​c+∇⋅j=0, where j\mathbf jj is particle flux, the number crossing unit area per unit time. A local linear response j=−D∇c\mathbf j=-D\nabla cj=−D∇c then yields the diffusion equation. This is Fick's law. Its minus sign does not give molecules a directional intention: more particles start on the concentrated side, so unbiased crossings leave a net imbalance. In interacting mixtures, chemical potential, the free-energy cost of adding particles, is the more general driving variable. A concentration gradient alone need not predict the flux.

The random-walk derivation makes its limits visible. Persistent velocities give ballistic motion at short times, with mean squared displacement proportional to t2t^2t2. Long waiting times, spatial obstacles, or long-lived correlations can prevent ordinary diffusion. Flow adds transport by the moving solvent, and reactions alter particle conservation. I therefore look for a time window in which displacement memory has decayed and an approximately constant DDD describes the measured spreading. In that window, the collective profile forgets most details of the microscopic steps while retaining their accumulated variance.

Something I can try asking. How would you distinguish slow ordinary diffusion from a process whose mean squared displacement has a genuinely different time dependence?

05Sound: A disturbance moves while matter stays nearby

Established phenomenon · collective modes · conservation

A spoken word crosses a room much faster than the air from the speaker's mouth. What travels is a correlated pattern of compression and velocity. Individual air molecules undergo fast disordered motion, while the small average displacement associated with the sound remains local. I want an equation for that pattern without following any particular molecule.

Write the mass density as ρ0+δρ\rho_0+\delta\rhoρ0​+δρ and the pressure as p0+δpp_0+\delta pp0​+δp, where the subscript denotes a uniform equilibrium state. Let v\mathbf vv be the small local mean velocity. To first order, mass conservation and momentum balance give

∂tδρ+ρ0∇ ⁣⋅v=0,ρ0∂tv=−∇δp.\partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_0\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf v=0,\qquad \rho_0\partial_t\mathbf v=-\nabla\delta p.∂t​δρ+ρ0​∇⋅v=0,ρ0​∂t​v=−∇δp.

A compression changes pressure through the material's equation of state. For an approximately adiabatic sound disturbance, which exchanges negligible heat between neighboring compressed and expanded regions during a cycle, δp=cs2δρ\delta p=c_s^2\delta\rhoδp=cs2​δρ, with cs2=(∂p/∂ρ)sc_s^2=(\partial p/\partial\rho)_{s}cs2​=(∂p/∂ρ)s​ and sss the entropy per unit mass. Combining the equations produces ∂t2δρ=cs2∇2δρ\partial_t^2\delta\rho=c_s^2\nabla^2\delta\rho∂t2​δρ=cs2​∇2δρ. A pressure excess accelerates adjacent fluid; its motion builds the next compression.

For an ideal gas, cs2=γp0/ρ0c_s^2=\gamma p_0/\rho_0cs2​=γp0​/ρ0​, where γ=Cp/CV\gamma=C_p/C_Vγ=Cp​/CV​ is the ratio of heat capacities at constant pressure and volume. This clarifies why density alone cannot determine the speed: restoring stiffness matters too. A dense but hard-to-compress material may carry sound rapidly. The mode is collective because the phases of many local density and velocity changes fit one propagating solution. The wavelength is a property of their coordinated pattern, rather than a molecule's flight length.

The wave equation assumes small amplitudes and local equilibration on times shorter than the oscillation period. Viscosity and heat conduction attenuate real sound; strong compression makes the propagation speed amplitude dependent and can form a shock. If wavelengths approach the molecular mean free path, the average flight distance between collisions, the hydrodynamic derivation loses its basis. The successful wave description therefore selects both an observable and a range of scales. Beyond that range, I must restore the microscopic relaxation processes that were hidden inside the equation of state.

Something I can try asking. Which measurement would distinguish a change in sound speed caused by compressibility from one caused by density?

Sources and what they establish
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, I Ch. 47. Derivation of the acoustic wave equation and the adiabatic rather than isothermal sound speed.

06Viscosity: Friction without rubbing solid surfaces

Established phenomenon · coarse graining · conservation

I slide one plate over another with a fluid between them. Even when the plates never touch, a force opposes the motion. The fluid layers transfer momentum: a faster layer loses some of its directed motion to slower neighbors. Viscosity is the coefficient relating this momentum transfer to the rate at which the fluid is sheared, meaning that adjacent layers move at different velocities.

For a Newtonian fluid in a steady, simple shear flow, the constitutive relation is

σxy=η ∂yvx.\sigma_{xy}=\eta\,\partial_yv_x.σxy​=η∂y​vx​.

Here vxv_xvx​ is the mean velocity along the plates, yyy is distance across the gap, σxy\sigma_{xy}σxy​ is the tangential stress acting across a surface normal to yyy, and η\etaη is dynamic shear viscosity, measured in pascal seconds. For plate area AAA, gap hhh, and relative speed UUU, negligible slip at the surfaces gives a linear velocity profile and a required force magnitude F=ηAU/hF=\eta AU/hF=ηAU/h. “Newtonian” names this linear stress–strain-rate relation; it does not simply mean that the molecules obey Newton's laws.

The microscopic route differs among materials. In a dilute gas, molecules carry their momentum between collisions, producing the estimate η∼ρvthℓ\eta\sim\rho v_{\rm th}\ellη∼ρvth​ℓ, where ρ\rhoρ is mass density, vthv_{\rm th}vth​ a thermal speed, and ℓ\ellℓ a mean free path. This explains a useful surprise: increasing density can shorten the mean free path enough to compensate the extra momentum carriers. In a dense liquid, intermolecular forces and rearrangements dominate, so that gas estimate is not a general viscosity formula. Both routes yield the same leading continuum relation when stresses relax rapidly enough.

The work done by the plates becomes internal energy. In this simple shear, the dissipation rate per volume is η(∂yvx)2\eta(\partial_yv_x)^2η(∂y​vx​)2, which is nonnegative for a passive fluid. The associated momentum diffusivity is ν=η/ρ\nu=\eta/\rhoν=η/ρ. Polymer solutions and suspensions can remember deformation or change viscosity with shear rate; at molecular distances even local stress needs careful definition. The emerging coefficient summarizes otherwise inaccessible relaxation processes, but its dependence on temperature, frequency, and forcing still carries information about those processes.

Something I can try asking. What would a delayed stress response after stopping a plate reveal that a single constant viscosity cannot capture?

Sources and what they establish
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II §41–1 and §41–2. Definition of shear viscosity and the viscous stress tensor.
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, I Ch. 43. Molecular transport estimates, including momentum transport and viscosity.

07Elasticity: How a solid remembers its shape

Established phenomenon · constraints · collective modes

A metal rod returns nearly to its old length after a small pull. Its atoms were never fixed points; they vibrated before, during, and after the experiment. The shape memory instead comes from a stable collective arrangement and the free-energy cost of deforming it. I need to describe relative displacements, because moving the entire rod without changing its shape should cost no internal elastic energy.

Let u(r)\mathbf u(\mathbf r)u(r) be the displacement of material initially at position r\mathbf rr. For small deformations, the strain tensor is ϵij=(∂iuj+∂jui)/2\epsilon_{ij}=(\partial_i u_j+\partial_j u_i)/2ϵij​=(∂i​uj​+∂j​ui​)/2. It removes a small rigid rotation and measures changes of lengths and angles. Expanding free energy about an unstressed stable configuration gives

F−F0=12∫Cijklϵijϵkl dV,σij=Cijklϵkl.F-F_0=\frac12\int C_{ijkl}\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{kl}\,dV,\qquad \sigma_{ij}=C_{ijkl}\epsilon_{kl}.F−F0​=21​∫Cijkl​ϵij​ϵkl​dV,σij​=Cijkl​ϵkl​.

Repeated indices are summed. The coefficients CijklC_{ijkl}Cijkl​ are elastic stiffnesses; σij\sigma_{ij}σij​ is stress, the iii-directed force per area across a surface normal to direction jjj. The linear stress law follows from the quadratic free-energy term, rather than requiring every atomic bond to be an exactly linear spring.

For an isotropic solid, whose response is independent of direction, two independent moduli suffice: one penalizes volume change, the other shear. In a crystal, the lattice symmetry generally permits more independent stiffnesses. Atomic interactions supply restoring forces, but thermal fluctuations and internal relaxation also affect the measured coefficients. Rubber gives a particularly useful warning against a purely bond-energy picture: stretching a network reduces the number of accessible polymer configurations, so entropy can provide much of the restoring force.

Static shear rigidity distinguishes a solid on the measurement time scale from an ordinary fluid, which continually rearranges under shear. Glasses can be rigid without crystalline periodicity, and viscoelastic materials combine reversible deformation with time-dependent flow. At large strains, defects move, bonds break, or rearrangements produce permanent deformation, outside the small-strain expansion. The emergent object is thus a displacement field with a reproducible restoring law, sustained by constraints that persist long enough for the experiment. Asking how long they persist is as important as asking how stiff each microscopic bond is.

Something I can try asking. If a material returns after a fast pull but flows under a slow load, which time scale must an elastic description include?

Sources and what they establish
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II Ch. 39. Elastic tensor, quadratic strain energy, microscopic stiffness, and limits of Hooke’s law.
  • MIT, Electronic and Mechanical Properties of Materials, Elasticity lectures. Authoritative course notes distinguish bonding-based elasticity in crystals and glasses from entropic elasticity in rubber.

08Surface tension: Why a drop behaves as if it has a skin

Established phenomenon · coarse graining · constraints

A small isolated drop rounds itself even though its surface contains the same molecules as its interior. I do not need to imagine a separate elastic wrapper. Molecules near the interface have a different neighborhood, and creating more interface changes the free energy. Surface tension γ\gammaγ measures that reversible free-energy cost per unit area under specified thermodynamic conditions.

For a clean interface with approximately constant γ\gammaγ, the surface contribution is Fs=γAF_s=\gamma AFs​=γA, where AAA is area. Consider a spherical drop of radius RRR. Increasing its radius changes area and volume by dA=8πR dRdA=8\pi R\,dRdA=8πRdR and dV=4πR2 dRdV=4\pi R^2\,dRdV=4πR2dR. Balancing the surface cost against pressure work gives

Δp dV=γ dA,Δp=2γR.\Delta p\,dV=\gamma\,dA,\qquad \Delta p=\frac{2\gamma}{R}.ΔpdV=γdA,Δp=R2γ​.

The pressure inside exceeds that outside by Δp\Delta pΔp. This is the spherical Young–Laplace relation for one interface; a thin soap bubble has two interfaces and a different factor. More generally, two principal curvatures determine the pressure jump. A smaller drop therefore needs a larger pressure difference to support its more strongly curved surface.

Why is a sphere selected? At fixed volume it minimizes surface area, provided other energies and constraints can be neglected. Gravity competes with surface tension over the capillary length ℓc=γ/(Δρg)\ell_c=\sqrt{\gamma/(\Delta\rho g)}ℓc​=γ/(Δρg)​, where Δρ\Delta\rhoΔρ is the density difference between phases and ggg gravitational acceleration. Drops much smaller than this length are shaped mainly by surface energy; larger drops flatten. On a solid substrate, the free energies of three interfaces also select a contact angle, so a free sphere is no longer the appropriate comparison.

The surface coefficient includes energetic and entropic contributions. “Missing neighbors” is a useful molecular starting picture, but does not calculate the full tension or explain every interface. Dissolved molecules that accumulate at the surface can change γ\gammaγ; gradients of tension then drive fluid motion. At radii comparable with the interfacial thickness, treating the boundary as an infinitely thin surface with a constant coefficient becomes inaccurate. Surface tension is an effective property of an interfacial region, made useful by a separation between molecular thickness and macroscopic curvature.

Something I can try asking. At what drop size should gravity noticeably defeat rounding, and which independently measurable quantities set that size?

Sources and what they establish
  • MIT, Advanced Fluid Dynamics, Section 11: Surface Tension. Official course notes identify energetic/mechanical definitions, Young–Laplace balance, and gravity and wetting effects.
  • Bush, Interfacial Phenomena, Lecture 3: Fluid Statics. Derives curvature-pressure balance and the capillary length for a meniscus.

09Screening: How many charges hide one charge

Established phenomenon · feedback · collective modes

A point charge in vacuum produces a potential proportional to 1/r1/r1/r. Put it in a dilute electrolyte, and the potential can decay much faster. The microscopic electric force has not changed. Mobile ions redistribute: opposite charges accumulate nearby, like charges are depleted, and their combined field weakens the original disturbance. Screening is this collective reduction of a perturbing field.

I use a symmetric electrolyte with charges +q+q+q and −q-q−q, each at bulk number density n0n_0n0​, in a solvent represented by permittivity ε\varepsilonε. At equilibrium temperature TTT, with Boltzmann's constant kBk_BkB​, dilute-ion Boltzmann distributions give n±=n0exp⁡(∓qϕ/kBT)n_\pm=n_0\exp(\mp q\phi/k_BT)n±​=n0​exp(∓qϕ/kB​T) for electric potential ϕ\phiϕ. When ∣qϕ∣≪kBT|q\phi|\ll k_BT∣qϕ∣≪kB​T, their net charge density is q(n+−n−)≃−2n0q2ϕ/(kBT)q(n_+-n_-)\simeq-2n_0q^2\phi/(k_BT)q(n+​−n−​)≃−2n0​q2ϕ/(kB​T). Poisson's equation then becomes, outside the inserted charge,

∇2ϕ=ϕλD2,λD=εkBT2n0q2.\nabla^2\phi=\frac{\phi}{\lambda_D^2},\qquad \lambda_D=\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon k_BT}{2n_0q^2}}.∇2ϕ=λD2​ϕ​,λD​=2n0​q2εkB​T​​.

The Debye length λD\lambda_DλD​ is the screening distance. For a weak point perturbation of charge QQQ, the three-dimensional solution is ϕ(r)=Qe−r/λD/(4πεr)\phi(r)=Qe^{-r/\lambda_D}/(4\pi\varepsilon r)ϕ(r)=Qe−r/λD​/(4πεr). Thermal spreading competes with electrostatic rearrangement: increasing temperature broadens the cloud, while increasing mobile-ion density shortens it.

The derivation is self-consistent. I first let the potential change the ion distribution, then include the field generated by that changed distribution. Using the bare charge's field throughout would miss the feedback. In a sufficiently large neutral system the screening cloud compensates the inserted charge, with boundaries and total-charge constraints determining where any remaining compensation resides. The response concerns the combined source and medium; it does not say that an individual ion loses its charge.

Linearization fails close to a strongly charged object. Finite ion sizes, strong correlations, and concentrated solutions can also invalidate the dilute mean-field description. Metals screen too, but their electron occupations obey quantum statistics, producing a different response law and sometimes oscillatory density patterns. I therefore treat the exponential form as a derived result for a specific regime, not a universal definition of screening. The broader emergent idea is that an interaction measured inside matter already contains the medium's organized response.

Something I can try asking. What change in the measured screening profile would show that a dilute, linear-response description has stopped being adequate?

Sources and what they establish
  • Hutchinson, Introduction to Plasma Physics I, §1.2.3: Debye Shielding. Official lecture materials cover Debye shielding; the two-mobile-species electrolyte coefficient is derived explicitly in this entry.

10Hydrodynamics: Why a few fields can replace an enormous state

Established phenomenon · conservation · coarse graining

A water flow contains an astronomical number of molecular coordinates, yet its large-scale motion can often be predicted from density, velocity, and temperature. I want to know why these variables survive when almost everything microscopic is discarded. The answer begins with conservation: a locally conserved quantity can leave a region only by crossing its boundary, so a long-wavelength imbalance generally relaxes slowly.

For an ordinary one-component fluid, mass, momentum, and energy provide the basic slow fields. Local equilibrium means that a small region has relaxed internally while remaining small compared with the scale over which the macroscopic fields vary. Its pressure can then be supplied by an equilibrium equation of state. Conservation of mass reads ∂tρ+∇ ⁣⋅(ρv)=0\partial_t\rho+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)=0∂t​ρ+∇⋅(ρv)=0, with mass density ρ\rhoρ and local mean velocity v\mathbf vv.

For an incompressible Newtonian fluid with constant ρ\rhoρ and shear viscosity η\etaη, momentum balance becomes

ρ[∂tv+(v ⁣⋅∇)v]=−∇p+η∇2v+f,∇ ⁣⋅v=0.\rho\big[\partial_t\mathbf v+(\mathbf v\!\cdot\nabla)\mathbf v\big]=-\nabla p+\eta\nabla^2\mathbf v+\mathbf f,\qquad \nabla\!\cdot\mathbf v=0.ρ[∂t​v+(v⋅∇)v]=−∇p+η∇2v+f,∇⋅v=0.

Here ppp is pressure and f\mathbf ff an external force per volume. The term (v ⁣⋅∇)v(\mathbf v\!\cdot\nabla)\mathbf v(v⋅∇)v accounts for acceleration caused by moving into a region with a different velocity, even in a steady flow. These are the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations. Conservation determines the balance structure; a constitutive assumption, the linear relation between viscous stress and velocity gradients, supplies the material closure. Conservation alone does not determine viscosity.

Hydrodynamics can therefore apply to chemically different liquids once their transport coefficients and boundary conditions are specified. The required separation of scales can fail near rarefied-gas boundaries, very rapid driving, or molecular confinement. Additional slow variables must be retained in mixtures, liquid crystals, or superfluids. Large-scale complexity is still possible: the nonlinear equations support vortices and turbulent motion. Emergence here means a controlled change of description, not an assurance that the resulting equations are easy to solve. I have replaced many fast variables with a small set of fields whose evolution is constrained by what the microscopic dynamics cannot quickly erase.

Something I can try asking. Which extra field would you need if a fluid contained a slowly relaxing molecular orientation in addition to conserved mass, momentum, and energy?

Sources and what they establish
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II Ch. 40. Derives continuity and material acceleration for continuum flow and states incompressibility assumptions.
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II §41–2. Adds viscous stress to momentum balance; source for the Newtonian constitutive relation.

Chapter 2

Collective order and its limits

A smooth continuum description can work without any special ordering transition. This chapter asks a different question: how do interactions select a collective arrangement, and how should I recognize it? A crystal repeats positions, a ferromagnet aligns moments, and an antiferromagnet alternates them. The same average that reveals one form of order can completely miss another. Choosing an order parameter is therefore already a physical argument about what the constituents are doing together.

I move from those examples to liquid crystals, where direction can remain ordered while position does not, and to phase separation, where composition becomes spatially nonuniform. Criticality then explains why fluctuations can grow across many scales. Universality asks why some of those fluctuations forget microscopic details and retain only a small set of structural distinctions.

The last entries test the limits of a simple symmetry-breaking account. Goldstone modes express the soft motions left by a broken continuous symmetry. The BKT transition reorganizes vortices without producing ordinary long-range order. Glasses become rigid on experimental time scales without a crystal lattice and without a universally settled equilibrium-transition explanation. These are related problems, but they are not interchangeable. Throughout, I separate the existence of a measured phenomenon from the domain of a model and from the stronger interpretation that a model might suggest.

11Crystallization: How a liquid chooses a lattice

Established phenomenon · symmetry · constraints

A liquid has no preferred origin for a repeating density pattern. A crystal does. Cooling can transform the same particles into a state with sharp diffraction peaks and a definite lattice orientation. I want to explain the change without saying that every atom simply finds its own lowest-energy position: the positions are selected together, and entropy remains part of the competition.

A useful observable is the static structure factor,

S(q)=1N⟨∣∑j=1Neiq⋅rj∣2⟩.S(\mathbf q)=\frac1N\left\langle\left|\sum_{j=1}^{N}e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r_j}\right|^2\right\rangle.S(q)=N1​⟨​j=1∑N​eiq⋅rj​​2⟩.

Here rj\mathbf r_jrj​ is particle jjj's position, q\mathbf qq is a scattering wavevector, and brackets mean an ensemble or suitable time average. When positions have a common periodic organization, amplitudes add coherently at reciprocal-lattice vectors, the wavevectors matching that periodicity. The resulting Bragg peaks reveal order over distances much larger than the particle spacing. A single particle cannot possess this relation among many positions.

At fixed temperature and pressure, the phase with lower Gibbs free energy is thermodynamically favored. A crystal may lower interaction energy enough to offset its smaller configurational entropy. Yet attraction is not necessary. Identical hard spheres, which only prohibit overlap, can crystallize at high density: an ordered arrangement can leave more total accessible motion than a crowded disordered one. This is a warning that visible spatial regularity and thermodynamic entropy are not opposites. The relevant count includes all allowed particle displacements, not just a snapshot's visual appearance.

A favorable bulk crystal need not appear immediately. In a simple nucleation model, a spherical crystal region in a metastable liquid has excess free energy ΔG(R)=4πR2γ−(4π/3)R3Δg\Delta G(R)=4\pi R^2\gamma-(4\pi/3)R^3\Delta gΔG(R)=4πR2γ−(4π/3)R3Δg, with interfacial tension γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 and bulk free-energy advantage per volume Δg>0\Delta g>0Δg>0. Small nuclei shrink because surface cost dominates; the barrier peaks at R=2γ/ΔgR=2\gamma/\Delta gR=2γ/Δg. Real nuclei may be nonspherical and grow on impurities, and rapid cooling can outrun crystallization entirely. Crystal order is therefore selected by thermodynamics but reached through kinetics. The emergent lattice must be distinguished from the route that created it and from the defects that the route leaves behind.

Something I can try asking. How could a purely repulsive particle system become more spatially ordered while increasing its total entropy?

  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II Ch. 30. Textbook explanation of crystal periodicity, reciprocal geometry, and defects; not used for the entropy-based hard-sphere argument.

12Ferromagnetism: A common direction without a common command

Established phenomenon · symmetry · collective modes

Iron can retain magnetization after an applied field is removed. The atoms do not receive a continuing instruction to point one way, yet their magnetic moments sustain a collective orientation. I begin with the Ising model, a deliberate simplification in which each site carries a two-valued spin si=±1s_i=\pm1si​=±1, representing a moment constrained to one axis.

Its energy is

H=−J∑⟨ij⟩sisj−h∑isi,m=1N∑i⟨si⟩.H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j-h\sum_i s_i,\qquad m=\frac1N\sum_i\langle s_i\rangle.H=−J⟨ij⟩∑​si​sj​−hi∑​si​,m=N1​i∑​⟨si​⟩.

The first sum runs over neighboring sites, J>0J>0J>0 favors parallel moments, and hhh is an applied-field energy per spin. The dimensionless magnetization mmm is an order parameter, an observable distinguishing the phases. At h=0h=0h=0, reversing every spin leaves the energy unchanged. Below the ordering temperature, a large sample can nevertheless settle into a state with either sign of mmm. This is spontaneous symmetry breaking: the equations retain a symmetry that a selected macroscopic state does not.

The energetic mechanism is local. Flipping a region inside an ordered state creates a boundary of unfavorable neighbor pairs. At sufficiently low temperature, the energy cost of these domain walls defeats the number of ways to place them. Raising temperature increases the statistical importance of disordered configurations. Replacing neighbors by their average gives the mean-field equation m=tanh⁡[(zJm+h)/(kBT)]m=\tanh[(zJm+h)/(k_BT)]m=tanh[(zJm+h)/(kB​T)], with coordination number zzz, temperature TTT, and Boltzmann's constant kBk_BkB​. It predicts ordering, but neglects spatial fluctuations. The nearest-neighbor chain has no finite-temperature ordered phase despite this approximation; the square-lattice model does. Dimensionality is part of the mechanism, not a decorative parameter.

In a finite zero-field system, averaging over both orientations gives m=0m=0m=0. Spontaneous magnetization is defined by taking the large-system limit before removing an arbitrarily small selecting field, or by identifying long-range spin correlations. Real ferromagnets also involve quantum exchange, magnetic anisotropy, and long-range magnetic fields. Multiple domains can lower the external field energy and make the total moment small even while each domain is ordered. The emergent property is cooperative magnetic order, with sample magnetization depending additionally on boundaries, history, and domain structure.

Something I can try asking. How would you distinguish a disordered zero-magnetization sample from an ordered sample containing equal opposite domains?

  • Tong, Statistical Field Theory, §1.1–§1.3. Lecture treatment of order parameters, mean-field theory, and the importance of dimensionality.

13Antiferromagnetism: Order that cancels its own average

Established phenomenon · symmetry · constraints

Suppose a magnetic material has almost no net moment. Is it disordered? Not necessarily: neighboring moments can alternate so regularly that the average cancels. I start with a lattice divided into two interpenetrating sublattices, AAA and BBB, with every nearest-neighbor bond connecting the two. The suitable observable must compare the sublattices rather than add them.

For localized moments represented by spin vectors Si\mathbf S_iSi​, the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model has H=J∑⟨ij⟩Si⋅SjH=J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_jH=J∑⟨ij⟩​Si​⋅Sj​, with J>0J>0J>0. Neighboring vectors lower their interaction energy by opposing one another. Define

M=1N∑i⟨Si⟩,L=1N∑iηi⟨Si⟩,\mathbf M=\frac1N\sum_i\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle,\qquad \mathbf L=\frac1N\sum_i\eta_i\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle,M=N1​i∑​⟨Si​⟩,L=N1​i∑​ηi​⟨Si​⟩,

where ηi=+1\eta_i=+1ηi​=+1 on AAA and −1-1−1 on BBB. The uniform magnetization M\mathbf MM can vanish while the staggered magnetization L\mathbf LL is nonzero. This alternating arrangement is Néel order. It creates magnetic scattering peaks at wavevectors matching the alternation, even when an ordinary magnetometer sees little moment.

A microscopic route to the sign of JJJ comes from electrons that hop between sites with amplitude ttt but pay repulsion energy UUU for double occupancy. At one electron per site and U≫tU\gg tU≫t, actual charge motion is suppressed. Brief virtual hops, intermediate states in quantum perturbation theory, still lower some spin configurations more than others. The resulting exchange scale is J≃4t2/UJ\simeq4t^2/UJ≃4t2/U for the simplest one-orbital model. Thus nearly immobile charge can support collective spin dynamics. Magnons, quantized waves of the ordered spin direction, carry energy without carrying a migrating lattice of electrons.

The two-sublattice picture is a starting point, not a universal outcome of repulsion. On a triangle, three moments cannot all be pairwise antiparallel; this incompatibility is frustration. Quantum fluctuations can destroy Néel order, especially for small spins in low dimensions. An exactly isotropic, short-range two-dimensional model lacks conventional spin order at nonzero temperature; real layered magnets can order through anisotropy or interlayer coupling. The lesson is that a vanishing simple average does not establish absence of order. I must identify the spatial pattern that the interaction actually favors and measure correlations adapted to it.

Something I can try asking. Which correlation measurement would detect alternating magnetic order when the total magnetization is exactly zero?

  • Hubbard (1963), Electron correlations in narrow energy bands. Primary interaction model underlying the stated large-U virtual-hopping argument; the exchange formula is a restricted strong-coupling consequence, not a general material law.

14Liquid crystals: Keeping direction while losing position

Established phenomenon · symmetry · constraints

A material can flow like a liquid and still distinguish one direction from another. I imagine many elongated molecules whose centers continually change neighbors but whose long axes tend to align. Translational order, a repeating positional pattern, has disappeared; orientational order remains. A nematic liquid crystal is the simplest phase with this combination.

For head–tail-symmetric rods, an axis pointing along n\mathbf nn represents the same orientation as one pointing along −n-\mathbf n−n. The average vector can therefore vanish in a perfectly aligned sample. I use a second-rank order tensor,

Qij=⟨uiuj−δij3⟩.Q_{ij}=\left\langle u_i u_j-\frac{\delta_{ij}}3\right\rangle.Qij​=⟨ui​uj​−3δij​​⟩.

Here u\mathbf uu is a molecular unit axis and δij\delta_{ij}δij​ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. An isotropic distribution gives Qij=0Q_{ij}=0Qij​=0. A uniaxial nematic has Qij=S(ninj−δij/3)Q_{ij}=S(n_i n_j-\delta_{ij}/3)Qij​=S(ni​nj​−δij​/3), defining the orientational order magnitude SSS and the director n\mathbf nn, an unoriented local axis. This observable respects the physical equivalence of a rod's two ends.

Alignment can arise from anisotropic attractions, but a particularly clean model uses hard rods that cannot overlap and otherwise do not interact. Two crossing rods exclude more positional volume than nearly parallel rods. At sufficient concentration, sacrificing some orientational freedom can increase the available freedom of their centers enough to favor alignment. Onsager's slender-rod theory makes this competition quantitative. The order is collective because the positional space available to one molecule depends on the orientations of its neighbors. It need not result from an explicit pairwise torque that always prefers parallel axes.

Slow spatial changes of n\mathbf nn cost elastic free energy, with distinct costs for splay, twist, and bend: respectively diverging axes, rotation around the local axis, and curved axes. An electric field or a boundary can orient the director, which explains how a flowing material can provide a controlled optical response. Defects occur where no smooth director can be continued around a loop. Real liquid crystals may be polar, layered, chiral, or composed of flexible molecules; the simple nematic tensor does not exhaust their order. This example teaches me to ask which symmetry has been lost before deciding whether a material should be called ordered or disordered.

Something I can try asking. Why is an average molecular axis insufficient to detect order in a head–tail-symmetric nematic?

Sources and what they establish
  • Onsager (1949), The Effects of Shape on the Interaction of Colloidal Particles. Foundational slender-rod model of orientational ordering from excluded volume; the approximation applies to sufficiently long, rigid rods.
  • MIT, Electromagnetic Energy: Liquid Crystal Display Technology, Lecture 26. Official lecture material on liquid-crystal structure, direction-dependent response, and electrically controlled orientation.
  • University of Michigan, Lecture 7: Excluded Volume. Authoritative lecture summary of Onsager’s hard-rod excluded-volume model and its self-consistent orientational distribution.

15Phase separation: When uniformity becomes unstable

Established phenomenon · instability · conservation

Mixing does not always smooth itself out. Cool a suitable binary mixture and a nearly uniform composition can separate into regions rich in one component or the other. I want to distinguish a state that merely prefers two phases from one in which an arbitrarily small composition fluctuation immediately grows. That distinction determines whether separation needs a rare nucleus or begins throughout the sample.

Let c(r)c(\mathbf r)c(r) be the dimensionless local fraction of one component. A minimal free-energy functional is

F[c]=∫[f(c)+κ2∣∇c∣2]dV.F[c]=\int\left[f(c)+\frac\kappa2|\nabla c|^2\right]dV.F[c]=∫[f(c)+2κ​∣∇c∣2]dV.

The bulk free-energy density fff represents local mixing thermodynamics, and κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 penalizes composition gradients. The corresponding variational chemical potential is μ=δF/δc=f′(c)−κ∇2c\mu=\delta F/\delta c=f'(c)-\kappa\nabla^2cμ=δF/δc=f′(c)−κ∇2c; with this normalization it has units of energy per volume. A positive mobility MMM converts chemical-potential gradients into flux. Conserved relaxational dynamics then gives ∂tc=M∇2μ\partial_tc=M\nabla^2\mu∂t​c=M∇2μ, the constant-mobility Cahn–Hilliard equation.

To test stability, I perturb a uniform composition c0c_0c0​ by a Fourier component with wavevector k\mathbf kk. Its growth rate is λ(k)=−Mk2[f′′(c0)+κk2]\lambda(k)=-Mk^2[f''(c_0)+\kappa k^2]λ(k)=−Mk2[f′′(c0​)+κk2], where k=∣k∣k=|\mathbf k|k=∣k∣. If f′′(c0)<0f''(c_0)<0f′′(c0​)<0, sufficiently long waves grow: a local enrichment lowers free energy and draws in more of the same component. This is spinodal decomposition. The gradient penalty suppresses arbitrarily short waves, selecting an initial domain scale. Under closed or periodic boundaries, the same equation conserves the mean composition and satisfies dF/dt=−M∫∣∇μ∣2dV≤0dF/dt=-M\int|\nabla\mu|^2dV\leq0dF/dt=−M∫∣∇μ∣2dV≤0.

The initial wavelength is not generally the final domain size. Regions often coarsen as material transfers to reduce interfacial area. Outside the spinodal region, a uniform state can remain locally stable even when a two-phase mixture has lower free energy; then a finite fluctuation must cross a nucleation barrier. Flow, elastic stresses, chemical reactions, and long-range interactions can alter or arrest coarsening. This model supplies a mechanism for one class of separation, with its assumptions visible. It does not imply that every patchy mixture has reached equilibrium or that every observed domain pattern arose through the same instability.

Something I can try asking. Which early-time observation would distinguish spontaneous growth of small fluctuations from nucleation across a free-energy barrier?

16Criticality: Fluctuations that lose a preferred size

Established phenomenon · collective modes · instability

Near the liquid–gas critical point, a transparent fluid can turn cloudy without filling with ordinary droplets of a separate phase. Density variations have grown large enough to scatter visible light. I begin with those variations rather than with a singular thermodynamic formula. A critical point is a special endpoint or continuous transition at which correlations extend to arbitrarily large distances in an ideal infinite equilibrium system.

For a scalar local order parameter ϕ(r)\phi(\mathbf r)ϕ(r), define the connected correlation function G(r)=⟨ϕ(r)ϕ(0)⟩−⟨ϕ⟩2G(r)=\langle\phi(\mathbf r)\phi(0)\rangle-\langle\phi\rangle^2G(r)=⟨ϕ(r)ϕ(0)⟩−⟨ϕ⟩2. “Connected” removes the contribution of the mean value. Away from the critical point, correlations typically decay exponentially beyond a correlation length ξ\xiξ. Near a conventional short-range critical point,

ξ∼∣t∣−ν,G(r)∼r−(d−2+η)(a≪r≪ξ).\xi\sim|t|^{-\nu},\qquad G(r)\sim r^{-(d-2+\eta)}\quad(a\ll r\ll\xi).ξ∼∣t∣−ν,G(r)∼r−(d−2+η)(a≪r≪ξ).

Here t=(T−Tc)/Tct=(T-T_c)/T_ct=(T−Tc​)/Tc​ is reduced temperature, ddd spatial dimension, aaa a microscopic length, and ν\nuν and η\etaη are critical exponents. The power-law window grows as ξ\xiξ increases. Exact scale invariance belongs to the limiting critical description, not to every distance in a real sample.

A Gaussian approximation makes the mechanism tangible. Give a fluctuation free-energy cost F=12∫[r0ϕ2+κ∣∇ϕ∣2]dVF=\frac12\int[r_0\phi^2+\kappa|\nabla\phi|^2]dVF=21​∫[r0​ϕ2+κ∣∇ϕ∣2]dV, with r0>0r_0>0r0​>0 and κ>0\kappa>0κ>0. With Boltzmann's constant kBk_BkB​ and temperature TTT, a Fourier fluctuation of wave number kkk has a thermal variance proportional to kBT/(r0+κk2)k_BT/(r_0+\kappa k^2)kB​T/(r0​+κk2). As the local restoring coefficient r0r_0r0​ approaches zero, long waves become inexpensive and ξ=κ/r0\xi=\sqrt{\kappa/r_0}ξ=κ/r0​​ grows. Interactions among these large fluctuations change the exponents in many dimensions of physical interest; this simple model is explanatory, not quantitatively exact there.

Large correlated regions also make response large: changing a small external field can affect many degrees of freedom together. Relaxation commonly slows because a larger region must reorganize. Finite size, imperfect temperature control, and finite observation time round the ideal singularities. Power laws by themselves do not establish criticality; broad disorder or other mechanisms can imitate them. I look for a consistent account of correlations, response, scaling, and the relevant control parameter before identifying a measured system with a critical point.

Something I can try asking. What evidence beyond one fitted power law would establish that a growing correlation length controls a transition?

17Universality: Why different materials can share exponents

Established phenomenon · coarse graining · symmetry

A fluid near its liquid–gas critical point and a suitable uniaxial magnet contain entirely different microscopic objects. Nevertheless, their leading critical exponents can agree. I want to understand what is being forgotten and what survives. Universality means agreement of specified long-distance properties among systems, after nonuniversal units and amplitudes have been accounted for; it does not mean that their phase diagrams or microscopic motions are identical.

The renormalization group studies what happens when short-distance fluctuations are averaged out and lengths are rescaled. Each step changes the effective interaction strengths, or couplings. A fixed point is a description reproduced by this transformation. If two different microscopic models approach the same fixed point, their large-scale critical correlations acquire the same scaling structure.

Near a fixed point, a small change ggg in an effective coupling can transform as

g′≃byg,g'\simeq b^y g,g′≃byg,

where b>1b>1b>1 is the length rescaling factor. A positive exponent yyy makes the perturbation relevant: it grows under repeated coarse-graining and eventually changes the large-scale behavior. Negative yyy makes it irrelevant: its leading influence diminishes. A zero exponent is marginal and requires analysis beyond this linear equation. The temperature distance from criticality is usually relevant, explaining why reaching a critical point requires tuning. Many details of short-range interactions are irrelevant, explaining why different tuned systems can agree.

The surviving distinctions commonly include spatial dimension, order-parameter symmetry, interaction range, and certain conservation or disorder constraints. An ordinary scalar liquid–gas critical endpoint can share static Ising behavior with a uniaxial magnet after appropriate mixing of thermodynamic variables. Their dynamics need not share a class, because density and magnetization can obey different conservation laws. Long-range forces, disorder, or an extra soft field can change the fixed point. Finite experiments may also remain in a crossover regime, not yet close to the asymptotic exponents. The explanatory gain is selective: I can predict which changes matter at large scales only after identifying the fixed point and testing its stability. Calling two complicated systems “universal” without specifying observables and limiting conditions supplies no such prediction.

Something I can try asking. Which microscopic modification would be most likely to move two apparently similar transitions into different universality classes?

  • Tong, Statistical Field Theory, §3. Authoritative lecture definitions of fixed points and relevant, irrelevant, and marginal couplings.

18Goldstone modes: The soft motion left by a chosen direction

Established phenomenon · symmetry · collective modes

Suppose an ordered material chooses an orientation although its microscopic laws prefer none. Rotating the whole ordered state costs no energy. What happens if neighboring regions rotate by slightly different amounts? Their mismatch costs energy, but a variation spread over a very long distance can cost arbitrarily little per excitation. This is the origin of a Goldstone mode, a low-energy collective motion associated with spontaneous breaking of a continuous global symmetry.

I take an ordered phase described locally by an angle θ(r)\theta(\mathbf r)θ(r). A uniform shift of every angle changes no energy. The leading static cost must therefore depend on gradients, for example

F[θ]=K2∫∣∇θ∣2dV.F[\theta]=\frac K2\int|\nabla\theta|^2dV.F[θ]=2K​∫∣∇θ∣2dV.

The stiffness KKK measures the cost of spatial twists. A small sinusoidal distortion of wave number kkk has energy density proportional to Kk2Kk^2Kk2 times its squared amplitude. There is no nonzero restoring cost at k=0k=0k=0. If the dynamics also contains an inertial term with coefficient χ\chiχ, L=χ(∂tθ)2/2−K∣∇θ∣2/2\mathcal L=\chi(\partial_t\theta)^2/2-K|\nabla\theta|^2/2L=χ(∂t​θ)2/2−K∣∇θ∣2/2, the mode has frequency ω=K/χ ∣k∣\omega=\sqrt{K/\chi}\,|k|ω=K/χ​∣k∣. Here L\mathcal LL is Lagrangian density, and χ\chiχ specifies the inertia of the collective coordinate.

This construction explains a gapless mode, meaning that its excitation energy tends to zero as wavelength grows. It does not fix every Goldstone dispersion. An isotropic ferromagnet has a quadratic low-wave-number magnon dispersion, because the dynamics of its spin components differs from the assumed inertial angle model. In nonrelativistic systems, two broken symmetry generators can form one conjugate pair and produce fewer modes than a naive one-generator-one-mode count suggests. Crystalline phonons require additional care because translations and rotations are spatial symmetries with dependent displacement descriptions.

Explicit symmetry breaking changes the conclusion: a preferred direction adds a restoring term for uniform rotation and can open a gap. Long-range interactions and coupling to dynamical gauge fields also alter the assumptions of the elementary argument. Low-dimensional thermal fluctuations can prevent the presumed ordered state from existing. I therefore first identify the symmetry, the actual order, and the dynamics. Only then does the soft collective coordinate become a prediction rather than a label attached to any low-frequency motion.

Something I can try asking. How would a weak field selecting one orientation change the long-wavelength spectrum of an otherwise freely rotating order parameter?

  • Watanabe and Murayama (2013), Redundancies in Nambu-Goldstone Bosons. Primary explanation of why broken crystal rotations do not require independent modes beyond phonons.

19Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition: A transition made by unbinding vortices

Established phenomenon · topology · collective modes

Can a two-dimensional magnet undergo a sharp transition without acquiring a nonzero uniform magnetization? I consider planar spins, each described by an angle θ\thetaθ, with short-range interactions favoring nearby alignment. At nonzero temperature, long-wavelength angle fluctuations prevent conventional long-range order in the ideal infinite isotropic system. Yet the low-temperature and high-temperature states can still be distinct because of vortices.

A vortex is a configuration whose angle winds through 2πq2\pi q2πq on a loop around its core, with integer winding number qqq. Smooth deformations cannot change that integer without moving a core through the loop or disrupting the field. With phase stiffness ρs\rho_sρs​, the long-distance free energy is F=(ρs/2)∫∣∇θ∣2d2rF=(\rho_s/2)\int|\nabla\theta|^2d^2rF=(ρs​/2)∫∣∇θ∣2d2r. A unit vortex has ∣∇θ∣=1/r|\nabla\theta|=1/r∣∇θ∣=1/r outside a core of radius aaa, giving

Ev≃πρsln⁡(L/a)+Ecore.E_v\simeq\pi\rho_s\ln(L/a)+E_{\rm core}.Ev​≃πρs​ln(L/a)+Ecore​.

Here LLL is system size and EcoreE_{\rm core}Ecore​ the nonuniversal core cost. There are of order (L/a)2(L/a)^2(L/a)2 possible vortex positions, so their positional entropy contributes approximately 2kBln⁡(L/a)2k_B\ln(L/a)2kB​ln(L/a), with Boltzmann's constant kBk_BkB​. Energy and entropy thus compete at the same logarithmic order.

At low temperature, oppositely winding vortices remain bound in pairs. Smooth fluctuations still weaken angle correlations with distance, but only as a power law: this is quasi-long-range order. Above the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition, free vortices proliferate and correlations decay exponentially. The crude single-vortex argument locates the competition; accounting for vortex pairs renormalizes the stiffness. The long-distance stiffness just below the transition obeys ρs(Tc−)=2kBTc/π\rho_s(T_c^-)=2k_BT_c/\piρs​(Tc−​)=2kB​Tc​/π in this normalization, the universal jump.

The same mechanism applies to appropriate two-dimensional neutral superfluids, with their phase replacing the spin angle. Finite system size, anisotropy, coupling between layers, and electromagnetic screening in charged films require separate analysis. A rounded crossover in a small sample is not by itself proof of the infinite-system transition. The topology here concerns classical winding defects; it should not be confused with intrinsic quantum topological order. The lesson is that the right distinction between phases can reside in which defects remain bound, even when a familiar average stays zero on both sides.

Something I can try asking. How could measurements of both vortex separation and long-distance correlations distinguish the two sides of a BKT transition?

  • Nelson and Kosterlitz (1977), Universal Jump in the Superfluid Density of Two-Dimensional Superfluids. Primary prediction of the universal jump in the renormalized stiffness.

20Glasses: Rigidity without a repeating pattern

Established phenomenon · constraints · disorder

A window supports shear, but its atoms do not form the repeating pattern of an ordinary crystal. I can understand this first as a competition of time scales. As a liquid is cooled while crystallization is avoided, its structural relaxation time τα\tau_\alphaτα​, the time needed to substantially rearrange its local environment, can become longer than the experiment. The material then appears mechanically solid even though its structure remains amorphous, meaning without long-range crystalline periodicity.

The operational glass transition occurs when τα(T)\tau_\alpha(T)τα​(T) becomes comparable with a preparation or measurement time tobst_{\rm obs}tobs​. That condition explains why the reported glass-transition temperature depends on cooling rate. A sample driven out of equilibrium can subsequently age: its responses change with the time elapsed since preparation. This differs from identifying a unique equilibrium phase boundary from a thermodynamic singularity.

The microscopic slowdown is collective. One particle may be confined by neighbors, and escaping that cage requires others to rearrange. To describe spatial variations in mobility, let wi(t)w_i(t)wi​(t) equal one when particle iii has moved less than a chosen microscopic distance during time ttt, and zero otherwise. Define the overlap Q(t)=N−1∑iwi(t)Q(t)=N^{-1}\sum_iw_i(t)Q(t)=N−1∑i​wi​(t) and its fluctuation measure

χ4(t)=N[⟨Q(t)2⟩−⟨Q(t)⟩2].\chi_4(t)=N\big[\langle Q(t)^2\rangle-\langle Q(t)\rangle^2\big].χ4​(t)=N[⟨Q(t)2⟩−⟨Q(t)⟩2].

Independent rearrangements give a modest value; correlated groups can give a larger one. The result depends on the threshold, ensemble, and dynamics, so it is not automatically a unique correlation volume. Experiments and simulations nevertheless establish heterogeneous relaxation: different regions move on different time scales.

What produces the growing barriers remains a deeper question. Theories emphasize competing structures, cooperative activated rearrangements, or dynamical facilitation, in which one mobile region enables a neighbor to move. Kinetically constrained models demonstrate that slow heterogeneous motion can arise from restricted allowed moves even with simple equilibrium statistics. That model result does not establish one mechanism for every molecular glass. The existence and relevance of an ideal equilibrium glass transition remain distinct from the observed kinetic arrest. I can therefore explain why finite-time rigidity emerges while leaving the ultimate asymptotic theory open, and test proposed mechanisms by their additional predictions rather than by the mere presence of slow relaxation.

Something I can try asking. Which measurement could distinguish two theories that fit the same average relaxation time but predict different spatial patterns of motion?

Sources and what they establish
  • Berthier et al. (2005), Direct experimental evidence of a growing length scale accompanying the glass transition. Primary experimental evidence based on multipoint dynamical susceptibilities; does not prove a unique microscopic mechanism or an ideal equilibrium transition.
  • Garrahan and Chandler (2002), Geometrical explanation and scaling of dynamical heterogeneities in glass forming systems. Primary kinetically constrained model analysis; supports facilitation as an explicit mechanism in models, not as a universal established explanation.

Chapter 3

Quantum matter makes new excitations

The useful particles inside matter need not be the particles from which the matter was assembled. A phonon adds a quantum of coordinated atomic motion without adding an atom. A Fermi-liquid quasiparticle retains an electron's charge while acquiring a different dispersion and lifetime. A fractional quantum Hall quasihole goes further: its charge and exchange behavior belong to a rearrangement of a correlated state. I will distinguish those constructions rather than use “quasiparticle” as an explanation by itself.

The chapter starts with durable low-energy excitations, then turns to macroscopic quantum organization. Bose condensation concerns occupation of a one-particle state; superfluidity concerns phase rigidity and persistent flow; superconductivity adds the electromagnetic response of charged pairs. Their connections are powerful, but their definitions and experimental tests are different.

Mott insulation and Anderson localization show two distinct ways to prevent transport, one driven by interactions and the other by coherent scattering from disorder. The final entries ask how quantum states can carry structure beyond ordinary local order parameters, and how a bulk topological distinction constrains a boundary. The common question is operational: which excitation, response, or state distinction becomes reliable at low energy? Each answer requires its own gap, symmetry, dimensionality, or time-scale assumptions. Quantum mechanics supplies the framework, while collective organization determines what its effective objects actually are.

21Fermi liquid: Why interacting electrons can look nearly free

Established phenomenon · constraints · collective modes

Electrons in a metal repel one another strongly, yet many low-temperature measurements look remarkably like those of an ideal electron gas with altered parameters. I would not infer that the repulsion has disappeared. Landau's Fermi-liquid description says that the low-energy excitations can instead behave like long-lived particles dressed by the response of their neighbors.

Fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle: identical fermions cannot occupy the same one-particle quantum state. At zero temperature, a noninteracting gas fills momentum states up to a boundary called the Fermi surface. In a Fermi liquid, a corresponding surface remains, and adding a particle near it creates a quasiparticle, an excitation with a sufficiently sharp energy and long lifetime to admit a particle description. It carries the electron's charge and spin, but its velocity and interactions need not equal those of a bare electron.

Landau organizes a small change of the many-body energy in terms of occupation changes δnp\delta n_{\mathbf p}δnp​:

δE=∑pϵp∗δnp+12V∑p,p′fpp′δnpδnp′.\delta E=\sum_{\mathbf p}\epsilon^*_{\mathbf p}\delta n_{\mathbf p}+\frac{1}{2V}\sum_{\mathbf p,\mathbf p'}f_{\mathbf p\mathbf p'}\delta n_{\mathbf p}\delta n_{\mathbf p'}.δE=p∑​ϵp∗​δnp​+2V1​p,p′∑​fpp′​δnp​δnp′​.

Here VVV is volume, ϵp∗\epsilon^*_{\mathbf p}ϵp∗​ is the quasiparticle energy, and fff parametrizes residual interactions; spin labels are suppressed. This is an effective expansion near the ground state, not a replacement of the full electronic Hamiltonian. The interaction term explains why compressibility and magnetic response are not fixed by a renormalized mass alone.

Why can a quasiparticle survive? Near the Fermi surface, occupied states block most final scattering states. In a conventional three-dimensional Fermi liquid, its energy width scales as Γ∝ϵ2+(πkBT)2\Gamma\propto\epsilon^2+(\pi k_BT)^2Γ∝ϵ2+(πkB​T)2, with ϵ\epsilonϵ measured from the chemical potential, the energy cost of adding a particle, TTT temperature, and kBk_BkB​ Boltzmann's constant. Thus Γ/∣ϵ∣\Gamma/|\epsilon|Γ/∣ϵ∣ vanishes as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0 at zero temperature. The excitation becomes better defined at lower energy. This supports a heat capacity proportional to temperature, with a coefficient determined by the quasiparticle density of states.

The description can fail in one-dimensional interacting conductors, near certain quantum critical points, or when another ordered phase intervenes. It is not a claim that every metal is a Fermi liquid. Its striking content is that interactions can reorganize the many-body state while leaving a tractable low-energy particle language. The test is the sharpness and consistency of the excitations, not whether the microscopic force happens to be weak.

Something I can try asking. What observation would show that an apparent electronic effective mass is no longer associated with a long-lived quasiparticle?

Sources and what they establish
  • Shankar (1994), Renormalization-group approach to interacting fermions. Author’s research account of the Fermi-liquid fixed point and instabilities; dimensional and low-energy restrictions matter.
  • Coleman, Many-Body Physics: The Unfinished Frontier. Authoritative lecture treatment of dressed fermionic quasiparticles and their low-energy description.

22Phonons: A particle made from many moving atoms

Established phenomenon · collective modes · coarse graining

A neutron can scatter from a crystal and lose a sharply defined amount of energy even though it has not created or removed an atom. The crystal has absorbed a phonon, one quantum of a collective vibrational mode. I want to see exactly what is quantized, because picturing a phonon as a tiny atomlike object hides the useful physics.

Take a periodic chain of atoms of mass MMM, spacing aaa, and nearest-neighbor spring constant κ\kappaκ. Let uju_juj​ be atom jjj's displacement and pjp_jpj​ its conjugate momentum. In the harmonic approximation, which keeps terms quadratic in the displacements,

H=∑j[pj22M+κ2(uj+1−uj)2],ωk=2κM∣sin⁡ka2∣.H=\sum_j\left[\frac{p_j^2}{2M}+\frac\kappa2(u_{j+1}-u_j)^2\right],\qquad \omega_k=2\sqrt{\frac\kappa M}\left|\sin\frac{ka}{2}\right|.H=j∑​[2Mpj2​​+2κ​(uj+1​−uj​)2],ωk​=2Mκ​​​sin2ka​​.

The allowed wave numbers kkk label normal modes, coordinated displacement patterns that oscillate independently in this approximation. Transforming to these coordinates turns the Hamiltonian into a sum of harmonic oscillators. Quantization gives mode energies ℏωk(nk+1/2)\hbar\omega_k(n_k+1/2)ℏωk​(nk​+1/2), with integer occupation nk≥0n_k\geq0nk​≥0 and reduced Planck constant ℏ\hbarℏ. Increasing nkn_knk​ by one adds a phonon and energy ℏωk\hbar\omega_kℏωk​.

A normal mode extends through the chain, but a superposition of nearby wave numbers can make a localized excitation packet. It propagates with group velocity dωk/dkd\omega_k/dkdωk​/dk when the packet is sufficiently narrow in wave number. No atom accompanies it across the crystal. A one-phonon number state has zero mean displacement; its extra energy appears in displacement and momentum fluctuations. A classical sound wave corresponds instead to a suitable coherent superposition of occupation numbers, which can have an oscillating mean displacement. These are related quantum states, not identical pictures.

At small ∣k∣a|k|a∣k∣a, the dispersion becomes ωk≃aκ/M∣k∣\omega_k\simeq a\sqrt{\kappa/M}|k|ωk​≃aκ/M​∣k∣, connecting the microscopic chain to continuum sound. Anharmonic interactions let phonons scatter and decay; disorder can also disrupt their motion. The phonon language remains most useful when the mode width is small relative to its frequency. Its crystal momentum ℏk\hbar kℏk is defined modulo a reciprocal-lattice vector and should not automatically be identified with the total mechanical momentum of the sample. The emerging particle is a durable pattern of excitation in the same atomic system.

Something I can try asking. Which measurement would distinguish a single-phonon packet from a classical lattice wave carrying the same mean energy?

23Bose–Einstein condensation: When one quantum state becomes macroscopic

Established phenomenon · constraints · collective modes

Cooling a gas normally narrows its momentum distribution smoothly. For bosons, particles whose many-body state is symmetric under exchange, a different possibility appears: a single one-particle state can acquire an occupation proportional to the total particle number. That is Bose–Einstein condensation. The atoms remain distinct constituents of a many-body system; they do not become one larger atom.

I start with an ideal uniform three-dimensional gas of particles of mass mmm and density nnn. Excited states have mean occupation [e(ϵ−μ)/(kBT)−1]−1[e^{(\epsilon-\mu)/(k_BT)}-1]^{-1}[e(ϵ−μ)/(kB​T)−1]−1, where ϵ\epsilonϵ is single-particle energy, μ\muμ the chemical potential or particle-addition energy, TTT temperature, and kBk_BkB​ Boltzmann's constant. Set the lowest energy to zero. As μ\muμ approaches zero from below, the excited states can accommodate at most

nex=ζ(3/2)λT3,λT=2πℏ2mkBT.n_{\rm ex}=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\lambda_T^3},\qquad \lambda_T=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\hbar^2}{mk_BT}}.nex​=λT3​ζ(3/2)​,λT​=mkB​T2πℏ2​​.

Here ℏ\hbarℏ is reduced Planck's constant, λT\lambda_TλT​ is the thermal wavelength, and ζ(3/2)=∑j=1∞j−3/2\zeta(3/2)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}j^{-3/2}ζ(3/2)=∑j=1∞​j−3/2. Below the temperature TcT_cTc​ at which nλT3=ζ(3/2)n\lambda_T^3=\zeta(3/2)nλT3​=ζ(3/2), the excess particles occupy the ground state macroscopically. In this model N0/N=1−(T/Tc)3/2N_0/N=1-(T/T_c)^{3/2}N0​/N=1−(T/Tc​)3/2, with N0N_0N0​ the ground-state population.

The mechanism is a saturation of available thermal occupations under Bose statistics. It requires no attraction in the ideal-gas calculation, although interactions and collisions matter for preparing and equilibrating real atomic samples. In a nonuniform or interacting system, a more general definition uses the one-particle density matrix, the amplitude correlation for removing a particle at one position and adding it at another. Condensation means that this matrix has an eigenvalue proportional to NNN. The associated eigenfunction identifies the macroscopically occupied orbital without assuming it is a zero-momentum plane wave.

Trapped rubidium experiments established condensation through a narrow component and its temperature-dependent occupation. The precise uniform-gas formulas above do not apply unchanged to a trap. Dimensionality matters too: a uniform ideal gas in one or two dimensions has no finite-temperature condensation in the thermodynamic limit. Finally, condensation and superfluidity are different questions. Occupation measures a property of the equilibrium state; persistent flow and phase rigidity concern response and dynamics. Their close connection in many interacting gases should not be used to make them identical by definition.

Something I can try asking. Why can a change in trap geometry alter the condensation threshold even when the atomic species and total particle number stay fixed?

  • Anderson et al. (1995), Observation of Bose-Einstein Condensation in a Dilute Atomic Vapor. Primary trapped-rubidium experiment; its evidence is not represented as a test of the uniform-gas condensate-fraction formula.

24Superfluidity: When flow cannot easily shed its energy

Established phenomenon · collective modes · constraints

A current normally decays because its organized motion excites other degrees of freedom. A superfluid can sustain persistent flow under appropriate conditions. I want to locate the obstruction to decay rather than describe the liquid as having no interactions. Interactions are precisely what can give the collective phase a stiffness and reshape the excitation spectrum so that slow flow cannot readily lose momentum.

Consider a homogeneous fluid moving relative to a weak obstacle. Creating an excitation with momentum p\mathbf pp and rest-frame energy ϵ(p)\epsilon(\mathbf p)ϵ(p) changes the relevant energy by ϵ(p)−v⋅p\epsilon(\mathbf p)-\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf pϵ(p)−v⋅p. If this is positive for every excitation, that emission channel cannot lower the energy. For an isotropic spectrum, Landau's criterion is

v<vL,vL=min⁡p>0ϵ(p)p.v<v_L,\qquad v_L=\min_{p>0}\frac{\epsilon(p)}p.v<vL​,vL​=p>0min​pϵ(p)​.

This is an energetic criterion for the specified excitation process. It does not prove that every real flow below vLv_LvL​ is immune to all dissipation.

A weakly interacting dilute Bose gas illustrates why interactions matter. With repulsive contact coupling g>0g>0g>0 and number density nnn, Bogoliubov's approximation gives ϵ(p)=[p2/(2m)][p2/(2m)+2gn]\epsilon(p)=\sqrt{[p^2/(2m)][p^2/(2m)+2gn]}ϵ(p)=[p2/(2m)][p2/(2m)+2gn]​, where mmm is particle mass. At low momentum, ϵ(p)≃cp\epsilon(p)\simeq cpϵ(p)≃cp with sound speed c=gn/mc=\sqrt{gn/m}c=gn/m​, so this excitation spectrum has vL=cv_L=cvL​=c. An ideal gas instead has quadratic excitations and zero value of this Landau threshold. Macroscopic ground-state occupation alone has not supplied protection for flow.

The superfluid velocity is related to an order-parameter phase by vs=(ℏ/m)∇θ\mathbf v_s=(\hbar/m)\nabla\thetavs​=(ℏ/m)∇θ for a neutral condensate of particles of mass mmm, with reduced Planck's constant ℏ\hbarℏ and h=2πℏh=2\pi\hbarh=2πℏ. Single-valuedness gives circulation in integer multiples of h/mh/mh/m around a loop that avoids vortex cores. Changing that winding requires a phase-slip process, such as a vortex crossing, rather than an arbitrarily small smooth relaxation. Obstacles, boundaries, temperature, and vortex nucleation can therefore set observed critical velocities below the simple spectral value. The superfluid fraction, defined through response to flow or rotation, also need not equal the condensate fraction. The emergent behavior is a constrained collective dynamics whose persistence depends on both the excitation spectrum and the accessible paths between flowing states.

Something I can try asking. Why can two channels containing the same superfluid have different measured critical velocities?

  • Floerchinger, Quantum Field Theory 1, Lecture 14. Authoritative derivation of the Bogoliubov dispersion and its Landau sound-speed threshold.
